title: When it hits
hookLine: the Buddha's two arrows: the pain, and what the mind adds; a neighbor in Islam: patience is at the first strike
tomorrow: an emperor at war kept his tools ready. what were they?

cards: A phone buzzes with bad news. Ten minutes later the mind is already racing: what if it gets worse, what should have been done, whose fault it is. The Buddha described that moment with an arrow.
Someone is struck by an arrow, and it hurts. Then, he says, they're struck by a second arrow, right after the first.

teach.b: Today's question: when pain hits, how much of it is the hit?
In the Sallatha Sutta, the Arrow, the Buddha says the untaught person, touched by a painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats the breast and grows distraught.
So they feel two pains, one in the body and one in the mind. Two arrows. The well-taught disciple feels the same first arrow; the Buddha doesn't pretend it away.
But they don't add the second.

One pain, not two. That's the Buddhist teaching: pain comes with a life; the piling on, the resisting and the story told about the pain, is the second arrow, and that's the part practice can work with.
Now a neighbor who shares it, in its own words. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, passed a woman weeping at a grave and told her to be patient.
Not knowing who he was, she snapped: you haven't been hit the way I have.
Later she came to apologize, and he said: patience is at the first strike. Shared: the moment right after the blow matters most. One honest difference.
In the hadith, that moment is met with sabr, patience that trusts God.
The Buddha names no God; he teaches seeing the feeling clearly, so the second arrow never leaves the bow.

how: Buddhist teachers use the simile of the two arrows to teach meeting pain without adding aversion and worry. Muslims are taught sabr, patience, and the hadith that patience is at the first strike of a calamity.

o: a sudden idea that changes everything
a sports injury that sidelines you
the moment hard news lands, and what you add

s: in the Arrow sutta, the wise feel no pain at all
they feel the first arrow; they don't add the second.
the Prophet told a grieving woman that patience is at the first strike
she snapped at him, not knowing him, and later came to apologize.
the Buddhist and Islamic teachings give the same reason for meeting the blow
the hadith's patience trusts God; the Buddha names no God and teaches seeing the feeling clearly.

games.q: your phone slips and the screen cracks an hour before a big video call. which response matches the Arrow sutta?
o: feel the annoyance, then fix what you can and take the call
pretend it doesn't bother you in the slightest
replay every clumsy thing you've done this year
games.why: the crack is the first arrow, and the annoyance is honest. the replay of every mistake is the second, and that's the one you can skip.

practice: Close your eyes and find one discomfort right now: a tight shoulder, a worry, a sore spot. Name it plainly, once: first arrow. Then watch for the second, the why me, the what if.
When it comes, let it pass by, and return to the breath.

wordCard.voice: When it hits: the Buddha's two arrows. The first is the pain, the second is what the mind adds, and practice is feeling one, not two.

orig.note: Pali: an arrow or dart, the image in the Sallatha Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: one arrow. The first one hurts; the second can fly past. Go easy today.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 36.6, Sallatha Sutta (the untaught person feels two pains, bodily and mental, as if shot by a second arrow; the well-taught feels one)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1283 (the woman weeping at a grave; 'patience is at the first stroke of a calamity')
